We review (and extend) the analysis of general theories of all interactions
(gravity included) where the mass scales are due to dimensional transmutation.
Quantum consistency requires the presence of terms in the action with four
derivatives of the metric. It is shown, nevertheless, how unitary is achieved
and the classical Ostrogradsky instabilities can be avoided. The
four-derivative terms also allow us to have a UV complete framework and a
naturally small ratio between the Higgs mass and the Planck scale. Moreover,
black holes of Einstein gravity with horizons smaller than a certain
(microscopic) scale are replaced by horizonless ultracompact objects that are
free from any singularity and have interesting phenomenological applications.
We also discuss the predictions that can be compared with observations of the
microwave background radiation anisotropies and find that this scenario is
viable and can be tested with future data. Finally, how strong phase
transitions can emerge in models of this type with approximate scale symmetry
and how to test them with GW detectors is reviewed and explained.

Human languages are complicated, and simply making the sounds required to say words and sentences involves a lot of very precise coordination. Your lips, jaw, tongue, vocal cords and diaphragm have to be controlled in very exact ways. Here, for example, is what you have to do to say the words "she sells": 1. Almost close your mouth, pull the tip of your tongue slightly back, let your tongue touch the roof of your mouth just behind your teeth. 2. Force air out from your lungs along a groove in your tongue and out between your teeth. 3. Open your mouth slightly, push the tip of your tongue forwards a little, but don't let it touch the roof of your mouth or your teeth. 4. Allow your vocal cords to vibrate while continuing to force air out. 5. Place the blade of the tongue against the ridge just behind the top row of teeth. 6. Continue to force air through over your tongue, but stop your vocal cords vibrating. 7. Open your mouth slightly further, take your tongue off that ridge behind your teeth and pull it back ever so slightly. 8. Start your vocal cords vibrating again. 9. Raise your tongue again exactly how far you raise it will depend on your accent, but it will probably rest against or near that ridge behind your teeth. 10. Keep your vocal cords vibrating, but you must force the air out around your tongue instead of over it. 11. Now move your tongue forwards slightly so that the blade is now resting against that ridge, allowing the air to once more flow over the tongue. That's just two words. There are a lot of muscles working together to do this, and because all these things have to be physically moved, it takes a certain amount of time. Tongue-twisters are deliberately constructed to make this is difficult as possible: the hardest tongue-twisters are those where the tongue is repeatedly being dragged back and forth, but not in a very regular rhythm. If you try to say these phrases too quickly, the signals from the brain are coming too fast for the different muscles to keep up. One of the classic tongue-twisters is this one: I'm not the pheasant-plucker, I'm the pheasant-plucker's mate. I am only plucking pheasants Because the pheasant-plucker's late. The key here is the alternation between "pl and "ph-," which is almost regular but not quite those sounds come in a different order in the third line. That messes up the usual pattern, and makes it very likely that, if you don't give yourself time to think, you'll get them the wrong way around in at least one of the lines, and hilarity will ensue.

The paper proposes to use reinforcement learning to learn how to compose the words in a sentence, i.e. parse tree, that can be helpful for the downstream tasks. To do that, the shift-reduce framework is employed and RL is used to learn the policy of the two actions SHIFT and REDUCE. The experiments on four datasets (SST, SICK, IMDB, and SNLI) show that the proposed approach outperformed the approach using predefined tree structures (e.g. left-to-right, right-to-left). 

The paper is well written and has two good points. Firstly, the idea of using RL to learn parse trees using downstream tasks is very interesting and novel. And employing the shift-reduce framework is a very smart choice because the set of actions is minimal (shift and reduce). Secondly, what shown in the paper somewhat confirms the need of parse trees. This is indeed interesting because of the current debate on whether syntax is helpful.

I have the following comments:
- it seems that the authors weren't aware of some recent work using RL to learn structures for composition, e.g. Andreas et al (2016).
- because different composition functions (e.g. LSTM, GRU, or classical recursive neural net) have different inductive biases, I was wondering if the tree structures found by the model would be independent from the composition function choice.
- because RNNs in theory are equivalent to Turing machines, I was wondering if restricting the expressiveness of the model (e.g. reducing the dimension) can help the model focus on discovering more helpful tree structures.

The present research is dedicated to provide deeper understanding of the
impact of complex architecture of branched polymers on their behaviour in
solvents. The folding dynamics of macromolecules and hydrodynamics of polymer
fluids are strongly dependent on size and shape measures of single
macromolecules, which in turn are determined by their topology. For this aim,
we use combination of analytical theory, based on path integration method, and
molecular dynamics simulations to study structural properties of complex
Gaussian polymers containing $f^c$ linear branches and $f^r$ closed loops
grafted to the central core. Using theory we determine the size measures such
as gyration radius $R_g$ and the hydrodynamic radii $R_H$, and obtain the
estimates for the size ratio $R_g /R_H$ with its dependence on the
functionality $f=f^c+f^r$ of grafted polymers. In particular, we obtain the
quantitative estimate of compactification (decrease of size measure) of such
complex polymer architectures with increasing number of closed loops $f^r$ as
compared with linear or star-shape molecules of the same total molecular
weight. Numerical simulations corroborate theoretical prediction that $R_g
/R_H$ decreases towards unity with increasing $f$. These findings provide
qualitative description of complex polymers with different arm architecture in
$\theta$ solutions.

>  Red, or dark meat is made up of muscles with fibers that are called slow-twitch. These muscles are used for extended periods of activity, such as standing or walking, and need a consistent energy source. The protein myoglobin stores oxygen in muscle cells, which use oxygen to extract the energy needed for constant activity. Myoglobin is a richly pigmented protein. The more myoglobin there is in the cells, the redder, or darker, the meat.
 >  
 >  When dark meat is cooked, myoglobin's color changes depending on what the meat's interior temperature is. Rare beef is cooked to 140° F, and myoglobin's red color remains unchanged. Above 140° F, myoglobin loses its ability to bind oxygen, and the iron atom at the center of its molecular structure loses an electron. This process forms a tan-colored compound called hemichrome, which gives medium-done meat its color. When the interior of the meat reaches 170° F, hemichrome levels rise, and the myoglobin becomes metmyoglobin, which gives well-done meat its brown-gray shade.



 >  White meat is made up of muscles with fibers that are called fast-twitch. Fast-twitch muscles are used for quick bursts of activity, such as fleeing from danger. These muscles get energy from glycogen, which is also stored in the muscles.
 >  
 >  White meat has a translucent "glassy" quality when it is raw. When it's cooked, the proteins denature and recombine, or coagulate, and the meat becomes opaque and whitish.
 >  
 >  Cows and pigs are both sources of dark meat, though pig is often called "the other white meat." Pigs' muscles do contain myoglobin, but the concentration is not as heavy as it is in beef. Chickens have a mixture of both dark and white meat, and fish is mainly white meat.

HIV Vaccine researcher here.

**HIV is Human Immunodeficiency Virus.** It's a virus which infects a certain type of white blood cell (mainly CD4+ T helper cells, but also monocytes, macrophage, and a lot of other cell types as well) making your immune system progressively weaker and weaker. When you lose too many key types of white blood cells (mostly CD4+ T helper cells), you are more susceptible to uncommon infections.

**AIDS is Acquired ImmunoDeficiency Syndrome**, and is the advanced stage of HIV infection. People with AIDS often see resurgence of chronic infections like Mono and opportunistic infections from stuff you get exposed to everyday like Toxoplasmosis. They also are more susceptible to certain cancers that your immune system otherwise would fight off, like Kaposi's sarcoma. What's worse: Defeating these infections is exceptionally challenging, as the lack of sufficient T-helper cells prevents a strong immune response.

Edit: Forgot to mention that there is **Another HIV-induced illness is HIV Neuropathy,** however this is distinct from AIDS in that it is believed to be more an effect of anti-HIV drugs than it is of chronic HIV infection. That being said, the precise mechanisms of HIV neuropathy are not completely understood, so it's still possible that the virus causes or contributes to neuropathy. This manifests in impaired sensation and motor function at the extremities.

**The treatment for HIV and AIDS is largely the same**: Drugs which shut down the HIV's ability to replicate, and drugs which boost the immune system to make more T-helper cells. But despite many treatment options, there is only one person currently considered to be "cured" of HIV: Timothy Ray Brown had a form of Leukemia that required a bone marrow transplant. He was also HIV positive. Following cancer therapies, it is believed every HIV positive cell in his body was destroyed, making him now HIV negative. He is still on life-long drugs to maintain his bone marrow transplants, but he does not require HIV treatments.

**Current research areas to facilitate cure are largely focused on eliminating HIV+ cells**: We have gotten really good at killing HIV replicating cells, but there are some cells that are HIV+ but don't actively produce more HIV most of the time. These are called HIV reservoirs, and we are focused largely on figuring out where they are and how to kill them. 

**HIV Prevention research** is focused on public health initiatives like condom use, and vaccine research (my area of specialty). To date, there has only been one vaccine regimen to show partial efficacy against HIV infection: the RV144 trial in Thailand, which achieved 32% efficacy over 5 years. Current efforts are underway to test a similar vaccine regimen in Sub-Saharan Africa, but it will be years before we know the efficacy of those trials.

Edit: For prevention, there's another vaccine-like strategy also being explored where instead of trying to get the immune system to target the HIV virions, you would reduce the number of immune cells in the genital tract. Upon exposure, the thought is that this would prevent an initial round of immune cells becoming infected and prevent the infection taking hold in the early stages.

We study randomized test-and-set (TAS) implementations from registers in the asynchronous shared memory model with n processes. We introduce the problem of group election , a natural variant of leader election, and propose a framework for the implementation of TAS objects from group election objects. We then present two group election algorithms, each yielding an efficient TAS implementation. The first implementation has expected max-step complexity O (log k) in the location-oblivious adversary model, and the second has expected max-step complexity O (log log k) against any readwrite-oblivious adversary, where k n is the contention. These algorithms improve the previous upper bound by Alistarh and Aspnes of O (log log n) expected max-step complexity in the oblivious adversary model. We also propose a modification to a TAS algorithm by Alistarh, Attiya, Gilbert, Giurgiu, and Guerraoui for the strong adaptive adversary, which improves its space complexity from super-linear to linear, while maintaining its O (log n) expected max-step complexity. We then describe how this algorithm can be combined with any randomized TAS algorithm that has expected max-step complexity T (n) in a weaker adversary model, so that the resulting algorithm has O (log n) expected max-step complexity against any strong adaptive adversary and O ( T (n in the weaker adversary model. Finally, we prove that for any randomized 2-process TAS algorithm, there exists a schedule determined by an oblivious adversary such that with probability at least 1 4 t one of the processes needs at least t steps to finish its TAS operation. This complements a lower bound by Attiya and Censor-Hillel on a similar problem for n 3 processes.

Integrated photonics is a powerful platform that can improve the performance
and stability of optical systems, while providing low-cost, small-footprint and
scalable alternatives to implementations based on free-space optics. While
great progress has been made on the development of low-loss integrated
photonics platforms at telecom wavelengths, visible wavelength range has
received less attention. Yet, many applications utilize visible or near-visible
light, including those in optical imaging, optogenetics, and quantum science
and technology. Here we demonstrate an ultra-low loss integrated visible
photonics platform based on thin film lithium niobate on insulator. Our
waveguides feature ultra-low propagation loss of 6 dB/m, while our microring
resonators have an intrinsic quality factor of 11 million, both measured at 637
nm wavelength. Additionally, we demonstrate an on-chip visible intensity
modulator with an electro-optic bandwidth of 10 GHz, limited by the detector
used. The ultra-low loss devices demonstrated in this work, together with the
strong second- and third-order nonlinearities in lithium niobate, open up new
opportunities for creating novel passive, and active devices for frequency
metrology and quantum information processing in the visible spectrum range.

The use of future contextual information is typically shown to be helpful for acoustic modeling. Recently, we proposed a RNN model called minimal gated recurrent unit with input projection (mGRUIP), in which a context module namely temporal convolution , is specifically designed to model the future context. This model, mGRUIP with context module (mGRUIP-Ctx), has been shown to be able of utilizing the future context effectively, meanwhile with quite low model latency and computation cost. In this paper, we continue to improve mGRUIP-Ctx with two revisions: applying BN methods and enlarging model context. Experimental results on two Mandarin ASR tasks (8400 hours and 60K hours) show that, the revised mGRUIP-Ctx outperform LSTM with a large margin (11 to 38). It even performs slightly better than a superior BLSTM on the 8400h task, with 33M less parameters and just 290ms model latency.

The Fomin-Kirillov algebra $\mathcal E_n$ is a noncommutative quadratic
algebra with a generator for every edge of the complete graph on $n$ vertices.
For any graph $G$ on $n$ vertices, we define $\mathcal E_G$ to be the
subalgebra of $\mathcal E_n$ generated by the edges of $G$. We show that these
algebras have many parallels with Coxeter groups and their nil-Coxeter
algebras: for instance, $\mathcal E_G$ is a free $\mathcal E_H$-module for any
$H\subseteq G$, and if $\mathcal E_G$ is finite-dimensional, then its Hilbert
series has symmetric coefficients. We determine explicit monomial bases and
Hilbert series for $\mathcal E_G$ when $G$ is a simply-laced finite Dynkin
diagram or a cycle, in particular showing that $\mathcal E_G$ is
finite-dimensional in these cases. We also present conjectures for the Hilbert
series of $\mathcal E_{\tilde{D}_n}$, $\mathcal E_{\tilde{E}_6}$, and $\mathcal
E_{\tilde{E}_7}$, as well as for which graphs $G$ on six vertices $\mathcal
E_G$ is finite-dimensional.

Another way to put it: How much mass could it accelerate from 0-60 mph in 2.5 seconds like a Porsche or Ferrari? Answer: A loaded freight train ~35 cars long.

---

Pounds of thrust is a force, so you can't convert it into horsepower or watts which are both units of power.

But let's say we put this force on a car and then reported its 0-60mph time. People like to have sporty cars that can do 0-60mph or 0-100km/h in [less than 3 seconds](_URL_2_).

Let's take the Saturn V thrust force and divide it by the average mass of a sports car, which seems to be around 1800kg. [The answer](_URL_4_) gives us an acceleration of 18900 m/s^2. That's an acceleration of 1900 *g*s. 

Using the old v = a*t equation, and plugging in 60mph as the final speed using that acceleration, we learn that the time to get from 0-60 is [1.4 milliseconds](_URL_3_).

Given that a blink of an eye is literally ~200 milliseconds, that's almost too fast to comprehend for me. So let's turn it around and ask how much mass could go from 0-60 in the 2.5 seconds of a very high end sports car? That becomes a 'solve for x' type equation that you learned about in algebra, and [the answer](_URL_0_) is 3.2 million kg.

So what is 3.2 million kg? Let's think about a [loaded train car](_URL_1_). How much do those weigh? The Internet seems to think a loaded train car is about 100 tons, so going with that, a Saturn V could accelerate a ~35-car fully loaded freight train from 0-60 in 2.5 seconds. That would be truly amazing and terrifying to watch.

---

Edit: Yes, these numbers are assuming your car magically pushes out this thrust without attaching the mass of the entire rocket to the car. This was just a fun thought experiment to put the amount of force in context to something you're more familiar with, not saying it's actually possible.

And for those saying sports cars are much less than 1800 kg, take that up with Wikipedia, I was just pulling an average curb weight from the cars in the table I listed above.

Tensor completion is a challenging problem with various applications. Many related models based on the low-rank prior of the tensor have been proposed. However, the low-rank prior may not be enough to recover the original tensor from the observed incomplete tensor. In this paper, we prose a tensor completion method by exploiting both the low-rank and sparse prior of tensor. Specifically, the tensor completion task can be formulated as a low-rank minimization problem with a sparse regularizer. The low-rank property is depicted by the tensor truncated nuclear norm based on tensor singular value decomposition (T-SVD) which is a better approximation of tensor tubal rank than tensor nuclear norm. While the sparse regularizer is imposed by a l 1 -norm in a discrete cosine transformation (DCT) domain, which can better employ the local sparse property of completed data. To solve the optimization problem, we employ an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) in which we only need to solve several subproblems which have closed-form solutions. Substantial experiments on real world images and videos show that the proposed method has better performances than the existing state-of-the-art methods.

Gravitationally collapsed objects are known to be biased tracers of an
underlying density contrast. Using symmetry arguments, generalised biasing
schemes have recently been developed to relate the halo density contrast
$\delta_h$ with the underlying density contrast $\delta$, divergence of
velocity $\theta$ and their higher-order derivatives. This is done by
constructing invariants such as $s, t, \psi,\eta$. We show how the generating
function formalism in Eulerian standard perturbation theory (SPT) can be used
to show that many of the additional terms based on extended Galilean and
Lifshitz symmetry actually do not make any contribution to the higher-order
statistics of biased tracers. Other terms can also be drastically simplified
allowing us to write the vertices associated with $\delta_h$ in terms of the
vertices of $\delta$ and $\theta$, the higher-order derivatives and the bias
coefficients. We also compute the cumulant correlators (CCs) for two different
tracer populations. These perturbative results are valid for tree-level
contributions but at an arbitrary order. We also take into account the
stochastic nature bias in our analysis. Extending previous results of a local
polynomial model of bias, we express the one-point cumulants ${\cal S}_N$ and
their two-point counterparts, the CCs i.e. ${\cal C}_{pq}$, of biased tracers
in terms of that of their underlying density contrast counterparts. As a
by-product of our calculation we also discuss the results using approximations
based on Lagrangian perturbation theory (LPT).

In the online packet scheduling problem with deadlines (PacketScheduling , for short), the goal is to schedule transmissions of packets that arrive over time in a network switch and need to be sent across a link. Each packet has a deadline, representing its urgency, and a non-negative weight, that represents its priority. Only one packet can be transmitted in any time slot, so, if the system is overloaded, some packets will inevitably miss their deadlines and be dropped. In this scenario, the natural objective is to compute a transmission schedule that maximizes the total weight of packets which are successfully transmitted. The problem is inherently online, with the scheduling decisions made without the knowledge of future packet arrivals. The central problem concerning PacketScheduling , that has been a subject of intensive study since 2001, is to determine the optimal competitive ratio of online algorithms, namely the worst-case ratio between the optimum total weight of a schedule (computed by an offline algorithm) and the weight of a schedule computed by a (deterministic) online algorithm. We solve this open problem by presenting a -competitive online algorithm for PacketScheduling (where 1.618 is the golden ratio), matching the previously established lower bound.

We approach the issue of the discovery of new physics at high energies
associated with the proposed International Linear Collider in the presence of
longitudinal as well as transverse electron and positron beam polarization. We
determine the beam polarization dependence and the angular distribution of a
particle of arbitrary spin in a one-particle inclusive final state produced in
e+ e- collisions through the interference of gamma or Z amplitude with the
amplitude from new interactions having arbitrary space-time structure. We thus
extend the results of Dass and Ross proposed at the time of the discovery of
neutral currents, to beyond the standard model currents. We also extend the
case of e+ e- annihilation in the s-channel to the production of bosons due to
t- and u-channel processes. Our work provides an approach to model-independent
determination of the space-time structure of beyond the standard model
interactions. We briefly discuss applications of the framework to popular
extensions of the standard model, and demonstrate that our framework is general
enough to account for certain results in the minimal supersymmetric standard
model.

There are two intriguing statements regarding the quantum cohomology of
partial flag varieties. The first one relates quantum cohomology to the
affinisation of Lie algebras and the homology of the affine Grassmannian, the
second one connects it with the geometry of quiver varieties. The connection
with the affine Grassmannian was first discussed in unpublished work of
Peterson and subsequently proved by Lam and Shimozono. The second development
is based on recent works of Nekrasov, Shatashvili and of Maulik, Okounkov
relating the quantum cohomology of Nakajima varieties with integrable systems
and quantum groups. In this article we explore for the simplest case, the
Grassmannian, the relation between the two approaches. We extend the definition
of the integrable systems called vicious and osculating walkers to the
equivariant setting and show that these models have simple expressions in a
particular representation of the affine nil-Hecke ring. We compare this
representation with the one introduced by Kostant and Kumar and later used by
Peterson in his approach to Schubert calculus. We reveal an underlying quantum
group structure in terms of Yang-Baxter algebras and relate them to Schur-Weyl
duality. We also derive new combinatorial results for equivariant Gromov-Witten
invariants such as an explicit determinant formula.

Economic Load Dispatch (ELD) is one of the essential components in power
system control and operation. Although conventional ELD formulation can be
solved using mathematical programming techniques, modern power system
introduces new models of the power units which are non-convex,
non-differentiable, and sometimes non-continuous. In order to solve such
non-convex ELD problems, in this paper we propose a new approach based on the
Social Spider Algorithm (SSA). The classical SSA is modified and enhanced to
adapt to the unique characteristics of ELD problems, e.g., valve-point effects,
multi-fuel operations, prohibited operating zones, and line losses. To
demonstrate the superiority of our proposed approach, five widely-adopted test
systems are employed and the simulation results are compared with the
state-of-the-art algorithms. In addition, the parameter sensitivity is
illustrated by a series of simulations. The simulation results show that SSA
can solve ELD problems effectively and efficiently.

In the very simplest form a cyclotron consists of two big circular magnets, one above the other ([Diagam](_URL_0_)). Charged particles sent between the two magnets will move in a circle because of the magnetic field between the two magnets. To provide acceleration there is a gap down the center of the cyclotron. As the particles move in their circular trajectory they will cross the gap twice every full orbit. The acceleration occurs because an the two sides of the gap are charged so an electric field sits across the gap. The trick now is that as the particles are accelerated they the radius of their orbit will grow larger and larger. However, they are speeding up so the time to complete a full orbit never changes. Because of this if you very the direction the electric field points in the gap you can time the change so that the particles always see an accelerating field on each pass.

That's the basic idea. Reality unforunately gets a little more complicated. Due to special relativity once the particles begin to reach higher velocities, relative to the speed of light the scaling between the radius of their path and the velocity becomes non-linear and things get much more complicated. The are two basic ways you can account for relativity. The synchrocyclotron which various the frequency of the electric field oscillations, or the isochronous cyclotron which modifies the magnets so that the field varies with radius.

Cyclotron originally saw a great deal of use in nuclear physics research though they are being phased out these days in favor of other types of accelerators. However, they still see a great deal of use in a variety of medical applications and there may even be growing demand for them once again if proton therapy takes off for cancer treatment.

Gas engines run on gasoline. They compress a fuel/air mix, which is ignited by a spark. They tend to have a broader useful power range, although this is very much dependent on the specific engine's design. Compression for this type of engine can be as low as 8:1 or as high as 12:1, and probably both lower and higher.
Diesel engines run on diesel fuel. They compress a fuel/air mix, which is ignited by the heat of the compression itself. They tend to have a narrower useful power range, again dependent on the engine's specific design. Compression in these engines is much higher than gas engines, usually 20:1 or more. 
Because diesel fuel has more energy in it, diesel cars tend to get better fuel economy than gas cars. Diesel engines tend to make more torque than gas engines, making them superior for towing or hauling.
Diesel engines have a reputation for being noisy and unrefined for passenger cars, and making a lot of bad-smelling smoke. In the US market in particular, there have been some very bad diesel engines over the years, and they have caused a public image problem for diesel. However, this is changing with newer designs and better fuels which contain less sulfur.

We consider 4-block $n$-fold integer programming, which can be written as
$\max\{w\cdot x: H x=b, l\le x\le u, x\in \mathbb{Z}^{N} \}$ where the
constraint matrix $H$ is composed of small submatrices $A,B,C,D$ such that the
first row of $H$ is $(C,D,D,\cdots,D)$, the first column of $H$ is
$(C,B,B,\cdots,B)$, the main diagonal of $H$ is $(C,A,A,\cdots,A)$, and all the
other entries are $0$. The special case where $B=C=0$ is known as $n$-fold
integer programming.
 Prior algorithmic results for 4-block $n$-fold integer programming and its
special cases usually take $\Delta$, the largest absolute value among entries
of $H$ as part of the parameters. In this paper, we explore the possibility of
getting rid of $\Delta$ from parameters, i.e., we are looking for algorithms
that runs polynomially in $\log\Delta$. We show that, assuming $\text{P}\neq
\text{NP}$, this is not possible even if $A=(1,1,\Delta)$ and $B=C=0$. However,
this becomes possible if $A=(1,1,\cdots,1)$ or $A\in \mathbb{Z}^{1\times 2}$,
or more generally if $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{s_A\times t_A} $ where $t_A=s_A+1$ and
the rank of matrix $A$ satisfies that $\text{rank}(A)=s_A$. More precisely,
 1. If $A=(1,\ldots,1)\in \mathbb{Z}^{1\times t_A} $, then 4-block $n$-fold IP
can be solved in $(t_A+t_B)^{O(t_A+t_B)}\cdot poly(n,\log\Delta)$ time.
 2. If $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{s_A\times t_A} $, $t_A=s_A+1$ and
$\text{rank}(A)=s_A$, then 4-block $n$-fold IP can be solved in
$(t_A+t_B)^{O(t_A+t_B)}\cdot n^{O(t_A)}\cdot poly(\log\Delta)$ time;
Specifically, if in addition we have $B=C=0$ (i.e., $n$-fold integer
programming), then it can be solved in linear time $n\cdot poly(t_A,\log
\Delta)$.

Under difficult environmental conditions, the view of RGB cameras may be restricted by fog, dust or difficult lighting situations. Because thermal cameras visualize thermal radiation, they are not subject to the same limitations as RGB cameras. However, because RGB and thermal imaging differ significantly in appearance, common, state-of-the-art feature descriptors are unsuitable for intermodal feature matching between these imaging modalities. As a consequence, visual maps created with an RGB camera can currently not be used for localization using a thermal camera. In this paper, we introduce the Semantic Deep Intermodal Feature Transfer (Se-DIFT), an approach for transferring image feature descriptors from the visual to the thermal spectrum and vice versa. For this purpose, we predict potential feature appearance in varying imaging modalities using a deep convolutional encoder-decoder architecture in combination with a global feature vector. Since the representation of a thermal image is not only affected by features which can be extracted from an RGB image, we introduce the global feature vector which augments the auto encoder's coding. The global feature vector contains additional information about the thermal history of a scene which is automatically extracted from external data sources. By augmenting the encoder's coding, we decrease the L1 error of the prediction by more than 7 compared to the prediction of a traditional U-Net architecture. To evaluate our approach, we match image feature descriptors detected in RGB and thermal images using Se-DIFT. Subsequently, we make a competitive comparison on the intermodal transferability of SIFT , SURF , and ORB features using our approach. As shown in the evaluation, feature matching using Se-DIFT results in a drastically increased area under curve (AUC) and decreased equal error rates (EER) of the receiver operator curves (ROC) for intermodal feature matching compared to a direct intermodal matching as well as matching based on intermodal predictions of other network architectures.

The junction forward voltage is the voltage applied to the emitter-base junction of a BJT in order to make the base conduct a specified current. The current increases exponentially as the junction forward voltage is increased. The values given in the table are typical for a current of 1 mA (the same values apply to semiconductor diodes). The lower the junction forward voltage the better, as this means that less power is required to "drive" the transistor. The junction forward voltage for a given current decreases with increase in temperature. For a typical silicon junction the change is 2.1 mVC. In some circuits special compensating elements (sensistors) must be used to compensate for such changes.

Like someone else mentioned, this seems to be a movie about existentialism. It's about trying to rationalize life and whatever meaning may be behind it. I think it also speaks on level about addiction, commitment, and development. We see Hoffman's character try to enact a play with the characters playing themselves, doing the things that they typically do. Hiring New Yorkers to live in his stage of New York. Actors start falling in love with the real version of their SO and blur the lines between reality and art. 
I interpret this whole sequence of actions as the continuous growth in people. One of my favorite quotes is from Camus: *a man defines himself by his make believe as well as his sincere impulses.* Even when we are stagnant, tiny aspects of ourselves are in continuous flux, even if they are not strongly attached to what we consider our identity. It's easier to see in certain characters in the movie, like Hoffman's estranged wife, Adele, who decides to run off to Europe (France?) to pursue a career and partake in a lesbian relationship. When we use acids in water , we like to compare the concentration of protons [ H+ ] . A really important concept when thinking about aqueous acids and bases is a physical constant called Kw , it 's 1x10 ^ -14 , and it is defined as [ H+][OH- ] , i.e the concentration of protons multiplied by the concentration of hydroxyl ( OH- ) ions . This allows us to easily convert between [ OH- ] and [ H+ ] , as their product is constant . If we have a 1.0 M of HCl , then we might anticipate that that will fully break up into H+ and Cl- , giving us [ H+]=1.0M. If we have 1.0 M of NaOH , then we might expect that to fully break up into Na+ and OH- . We want to be able to compare the acidity of the solutions though , so we can convert [ OH-]=1.0 into a value of [ H+ ] using Kw . [ H+ ] = Kw/[OH- ] Giving us , for 1.0 M NaOH , [ H+ ] = 1x10 ^ -14 . Now , 1 and 1x10 ^ -14 are very different numbers , and we 're humans - we like numbers that we can think about , like 6 or 12 or 241 . So we can squeeze this entire range into a much ' nicer ' range of numbers ( 0 to 14 - but I 'll explain that ) . In order to compress this range of orders of magnitude we must use a logarithmic scale . All this means is that when go from pH 1 to ph 2 , we are changing an order of magnitude , not a single digit . The process of taking the logarithm of a number means that you are asking the question ' What power do I have to raise 10 to in order to get this number ' i.e log(10 ^ 6 ) = 6 . pH is defined as -log[H+ ] . There are non - trivial things going on here - the negative sign . This means that the range goes from 0 to 14 , rather than from -14 to 0 . Like so many things in science , we have to define a direction , even though it does n't really matter : we often pick the one that is warmest and fuzziest ( 0 to 14 seems really nice , right ? ) and as long as you can learn and know that a low pH indicates more [ H+ ] than [ OH- ] , i.e. indicates acidic behaviour , then you can use and apply the pH scale as you wish . In general all programming languages can all do the exact same thing. They differ in how easy, how fast and how efficient the process of doing the thing is.  
The basic test for what a programming language can do is to see if it can do the same thing as a very simple computer called a "Turing machine" and language or system that can do that is called "Turing Complete". A language that is Turing Complete could do any computation task given an infinite amount of time and memory. This turns out to be a very low bar, for example people have built a turing complete computer inside of Minecraft.  
  
Once that low bar is out of the way the languages begin to differentiate.  
Some languages like Python are super easy to learn, but run really really slow. This allows you to focus on making you algorithm really good, but makes it nearly impossible to fiddle with the nuts and bolts of how the program is run.   
  
Some languages like C are more difficult to learn but run really fast. Alot of the old operating systems were coded in C, because they really need it going quickly.
  
Some language like Java or C++ strike a balance in between them.  
  
Other languages like MATLAB focus on doing one thing and doing it really really fast and easy, but are difficult for other thing. MATLAB does math and graphs really really well, but you would have to jump through some serious hoops to build a game out of it.  
  
Also the languages differ in the "Libraries" that support it. A libary is a collection of code that a programmer can call upon to help him do something. For example rather than writing the code to draw a cube on the screen from scratch, he downloads a library and calls the function in the library to do it for him.

When a cell phone pings a tower, it sends a very short message. But what it actually has to send is a packet: a larger (but still small) block of data. Many providers now support longer messages, but when one doesn't, or two providers don't work together well, it falls back on splitting it into the basic short message that they all support.

Embezzlement is taking funds that you been entrusted with, and converting them to your own use. Theft is just taking property to which you are not entitled. So, Janice is a teller at a bank. She's required to keep a drawer full of cash, count it, dispense it to customers as needed, etc. That money has been entrusted to her, so she's given access to it. If she were to take 20 from that drawer for herself, that'd be embezzlement. If she were to go into the McDonald's across the street and take 20 from their till while someone wasn't watching, that'd be theft.,Theft," generally speaking, is the term used to refer to the category of property crimes that involve taking other people's stuff for your own use without their permission. Crimes like "embezzlement," "shoplifting," "robbery," "larceny," "mugging," "carjacking," etc. are all different kinds of theft and are distinguished by the facts of the crime. For a property crime to be embezzlement, the defendant must have been entrusted with possession of the stolen property before the defendant decided to steal it. If the defendant did not have legitimate possession, then stealing it can't be embezzlement. It will be some other kind of property crime. Other theft crimes have different criteria. "Robbery" is usually defined as theft "by force or fear," usually implying that the victim has to be present. "Carjacking" is basically robbery, only the property being stolen is a car or other vehicle. "Shoplifting," sometimes also called "retail theft," is stealing inventory from a store. These distinctions are made because not all kinds of stealing are equally serious. Pocketing a candy bar from a convenience store is not as bad as robbing a bank at gunpoint, and neither is precisely the same as embezzling corporate funds.

You read out the ROM contents to a computer file. That file can then be edited. The results can't be uploaded back to the original ROM, because ROM means "Read Only Memory"...it can't be written. But you can get a replacement that instead uses an EEPROM ("Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory"), and those can be written many times, although relatively slowly. 
 
The biggest trick is to know how to edit the file to do what you want. The ROM contents are going to be stored in "machine language", the binary form of the instructions and data for a specific microcontroller or microprocessor. You need a "reverse assembler" or "reverse compiler" to convert that to assembly language or higher level programming language to make it more readable, and then you need to figure out what the program does, so that you can change the parts you want. Once you do, you change it and run the changed version back through an assembler or compiler and that's the file that you'll need to burn to the EEPROM. 
 
If you are dealing with a system with some security, there may be some more tricks you need to apply. One simple security method is to scramble the ROM contents, so that someone who reads them back in the "normal" way will read back garbled information. A more sophisticated method is to encrypt the ROM contents, so that even when correctly read out, it needs to be deciphered using a secret key (and the correct algorithm).

In this paper, we develop a Bayesian evidence maximization framework to solve the sparse non-negative least squares problem (S-NNLS). We introduce a family of scale mixtures referred as to Rectified Gaussian Scale Mixture (R-GSM) to model the sparsity enforcing prior distribution for the signal of interest. Through proper choice of the mixing density, the R-GSM prior encompasses a wide variety of heavy-tailed distributions such as the rectified Laplacian and rectified Student-t distributions. Utilizing the hierarchical representation induced by the scale mixture prior, an evidence maximization or Type II estimation method based on the expectation-maximization (EM) framework is developed to estimate the hyper-parameters and to obtain a point estimate of the parameter of interest. In the proposed method, called rectified Sparse Bayesian Learning (R-SBL), we provide four alternative approaches that offer a range of options to trade-off computational complexity to quality of the E-step computation. The methods include the Markov Chain Monte Carlo EM, linear minimum mean square estimation, approximate message passing and a diagonal approximation. Through numerical experiments, we show that the proposed R-SBL method outperforms existing S-NNLS solvers in terms of both signal and support recovery.

Massive MIMO is a promising technique to meet the exponential growth of global mobile data traffic demand. However, contrary to the current systems, energy consumption of next generation networks is required to be load adaptive as the network load varies significantly throughout the day. In this paper, we propose a load adaptive massive MIMO system that varies the number of antennas following the daily load profile (DLP) in order to maximize the downlink energy efficiency (EE). A multi-cell system is considered where each base station (BS) is equipped with a large number of antennas to serve many single antenna users. In order to incorporate DLP, each BS is modeled as an M G m m state dependent queue under the assumption that the network is dimensioned to serve a maximum number of users at the peak load. For a given number of users in a cell, the optimum number of active antennas maximizing EE is derived. The EE maximization problem is formulated in a game theoretic framework where the number of antennas to be used by a BS is determined through best response iteration. This load adaptive system achieves overall 19 higher EE compared to a baseline system where the BSs always run with the fixed number of antennas that is most energy efficient at peak load and that can be switched-off when there is no traffic.

The Electoral College represents a distinctive aspect of American democracy, playing a pivotal role in the presidential election process. Unlike direct popular elections where the candidate with the most votes wins, the U.S. employs this intermediary body consisting of electors. For a presidential hopeful to claim victory, they must secure a majority of electoral votes, with the magic number being 270 out of 538. 
Electors are chosen by political parties within each state, and their selection often reflects party loyalty and political clout. After the general populace casts their ballots on Election Day, it is these electors who ultimately vote for the president in December. Each state's electoral votes are commensurate with its representation in Congress, amalgamating the number of senators and representatives the state possesses.
The "Certificate of Ascertainment" plays an instrumental role in legitimizing the electors. This certificate, signed by the governor, confirms the election results in the state and lists the appointed electors. It marks a bureaucratic yet vital step in the chain of the electoral process, ensuring transparency and certitude in the eventual electoral tally.
However, the debate rages on whether the Electoral College should continue to be a feature of American elections. Opponents argue that it subverts the principle of "one person, one vote" by disproportionally empowering smaller states and sometimes contravening the popular vote, as witnessed in the 2000 and 2016 elections. They also posit that it leads to a focus on "swing states," effectively sidelining voters in solidly blue or red states.
While acknowledging these valid concerns, I argue in favor of maintaining the Electoral College. It buttresses the federal structure of the U.S., preserving the importance of states within a united republic. It prevents regional candidates from solely focusing on populous urban areas, thereby requiring a broader national coalition to win. The Electoral College fosters political stability and compels candidates to appeal to a diverse array of voters across the nation.
In conclusion, notwithstanding its imperfections and complexities, the Electoral College remains a core component of our federative political system. It reflects a balance between popular mandate and state representation, thus, it should be preserved, albeit with an open mind toward reforms that could enhance its alignment with contemporary democratic principles.

Espresso macarons are a decadent and delicious treat that are perfect for a special occasion or to impress your guests. They can also be a little intimidating to make, but with the right techniques, anyone can create these delicate and scrumptious treats. In this article, we will guide you through the process of making espresso macarons step-by-step.
Part 1: Preparing the Ingredients and Equipment
Before you start making the macarons, make sure you have the following ingredients and equipment:
Ingredients:
1 ½ cups almond flour
1 ¾ cups confectioner's sugar
3 large egg whites
1/3 cup granulated sugar
2 tablespoons instant-espresso powder
Equipment:
Food processor
Sieve
Electric mixer
Pastry bag with a tip
Baking sheets
Parchment paper
Part 2: Making the Macaron Shells
Preheat your oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit (178 Celsius). This will ensure that your oven is nice and hot, ready to bake the macarons.
Place your almonds in a food processor and pulse until they are finely ground.
Add confectioner's sugar to the food processor and pulse until the mixture is fine and well combined.
Put the mixture through a sieve and press down on the mixture to get rid of any lumps.
Repeat the grinding and sieving process until you have less than 2 tablespoons of solids left in the sieve. This will ensure that your macaron shells are smooth and consistent.
In a large mixing bowl, whisk egg whites and granulated sugar by hand until they are frothy. Then, using an electric mixer, beat the mixture for 6 minutes until it forms stiff peaks.
Add instant-espresso powder and continue beating until the mixture becomes glossy and forms stiff peaks again.
Pour the dry ingredients into the egg white mixture and fold it in using a spatula. Fold the mixture from the bottom of the bowl upward, then press the flat side of the spatula firmly through the middle of the mixture. Repeat until the mixture is smooth and shiny.
Rest a pastry bag inside a glass for easy filling. Transfer the batter to the pastry bag.
Prepare two baking sheets lined with parchment paper.
With the end of your piping tip about 1/2 inch above the sheet, pipe the batter into a 3/4-inch round shape. Pipe the macaron shells about 1-inch apart from each other.
Tap the baking sheet on the counter to release any air bubbles.
Sift espresso powder over half of the unbaked rounds.
Part 3: Baking and Filling the Macarons
Bake the macarons for 13 minutes or until the edges have formed a crispy shell and the center is no longer wet.
Let the cookies cool on the baking sheet. You can also use a spatula to transfer them to a wire rack.
While the cookies are cooling, prepare your filling. You can use a variety of fillings, such as ganache or buttercream, but for this recipe, we recommend espresso buttercream.
Once the macaron shells are cooled, spread your filling on one half of the cookies and top them with the other half of the cookies.
Serve and enjoy your delicious espresso macarons!
In conclusion, making espresso macarons requires patience and precision, but with the right techniques and equipment, anyone can recreate these delicate and scrumptious treats. We hope that this step-by-step guide has demystified the art of macaron-making and inspired you to try making your own espresso macarons at home.

We present the results of our study on the detection of very high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray emission from the distant blazar 1ES 1101-232 using the High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S.) and broadband characterisation. Blazars are active galactic nuclei with relativistic jets pointing towards the observer, making them significant sources of VHE gamma-rays. The detection of VHE gamma-ray emission from distant blazars provides valuable insight into the acceleration mechanisms of cosmic rays and the nature of extragalactic gamma-ray sources.

Our observations of 1ES 1101-232 with H.E.S.S. reveal a significant excess of gamma-ray events above background at energies above 200 GeV, with a statistical significance of 11.5 standard deviations. The measured flux at 300 GeV is (1.76 ± 0.14) × 10^-11 cm^-2 s^-1, making 1ES 1101-232 one of the most distant VHE gamma-ray sources detected to date. We also report on the spectral and temporal characteristics of the source, as well as its broadband spectral energy distribution.

Our results provide new constraints on the theoretical models describing blazar emission, and on the intergalactic background light (IBL), which affects gamma-ray propagation. The detection of VHE gamma-ray emission from this distant blazar highlights the capabilities of H.E.S.S. and sets the stage for future studies of distant extragalactic sources.

In this work, we investigate the temperature dependence of the tensile properties of single walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) through O(N) tight binding molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. SWCNTs exhibit exceptional mechanical properties such as high tensile strength and stiffness, and are therefore considered as potential building blocks for future nanoscale devices. However, it is crucial to understand how these properties vary with temperature as well. Our research attempts to fill this knowledge gap by exploring the influence of temperature on the mechanical properties of SWCNTs.Our comprehensive simulations reveal that the tensile properties of SWCNTs are highly sensitive to temperature. The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and Young's modulus decrease with increasing temperature, whereas the failure strain increases. This trend is observed for all chiralities of SWCNTs in our simulations. Our results suggest that temperature-induced disorder and thermal vibrations play a critical role in the mechanical properties of SWCNTs. Our study provides relevant insight into the mechanical performance of SWCNTs under different temperature conditions, essential for the design and optimization of nanoscale devices.

In embracing cell phones in an educational setting, we acknowledge the realities of the modern world. How to Wake up the Writer in You

Writing is both an art and a skill. It requires creativity, passion, and discipline. However, sometimes, it can be difficult to ignite that spark of inspiration and start writing. If you're struggling to find your voice, here are some tips on how to wake up the writer in you.

1. Watch a Historical Movie and Take Notes

The night before your "inspiration day," watch a historical movie and write down several stories that interested you within it. This can serve as a great source of inspiration for your writing. You can take inspiration from the characters, the settings, the themes, and even the cinematography.

2. Clear Your Mind

On the day you decide to write, clear your mind of everything that's been bothering you. Take some time to just sit outside or open your window and enjoy the fresh air. This can help you focus on your writing and get your creative juices flowing.

3. Make a List of Possible Characters

In a notebook, make a list of possible characters for your story. You can draw inspiration from the historical movie you watched or come up with your own unique characters. This can also be a good time to brainstorm possible subplots and themes.

4. Add Your Own Personal Touch

Give your story your own style and flair. Add personal touches that make it unique and special to you. This can be a great way to express yourself creatively and make your writing stand out.

5. Edit and Refine

After you've written your story, go back and edit it. Cross off any subplots, characters, or personal touches that don't add to the story or make it stronger. Feel free to take some time to daydream about how your story will go and refine it until you're happy with it.

In conclusion, writing can be a daunting task, but by following these steps, you can wake up the writer in you. Remember to find inspiration in the world around you, take the time to clear your mind, and give your writing your own personal touch. Happy writing!

If you are diagnosed with hypothyroidism, your doctor may recommend medication to help restore normal thyroid function. Taking synthetic thyroid hormones can usually resolve the issue.
In some cases, hypothyroidism may be caused by a problem with the pituitary gland, which controls the thyroid. If this is the case, surgery or radiation therapy may be needed to correct the underlying problem.
Overall, it is important to be aware of the signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism and to see a doctor if you think you may have the condition. With proper diagnosis and treatment, hypothyroidism can be well controlled and its symptoms improved.

The idea of making it mandatory for every student to participate in an after-school activity may seem laudable at first glance; however, upon closer examination, it becomes clear that such a policy would not be beneficial. This essay will explore the potential negative implications of mandatory participation, such as time management issues, lack of interest, and the strain on funds and workers, before proposing alternative solutions.
One of the primary concerns with making after-school participation mandatory is the issue of time management. Students already have a multitude of commitments, such as homework, studying for exams, and family obligations. Adding another obligation to their already overloaded schedules would leave students with little time for leisure or downtime, leading to increased stress levels and potential burnout. For example, a high school student may be involved in sports, music lessons, and extracurricular clubs, leaving little time for relaxation or spending time with family and friends. Forcing them to engage in yet another activity could have detrimental effects on their mental and physical well-being.
Moreover, mandatory participation fails to account for individual interests. Not all students have the same passions or abilities, and forcing them to participate in activities they have no interest in may breed resentment and disengagement. For instance, a student who excels in math but has little interest in arts and crafts may feel frustrated and demotivated if forced to attend an art club. This could create a negative association with extracurricular activities, leading to decreased participation and potential missed opportunities to explore their true passions and talents.
Furthermore, implementing mandatory participation requires adequate funds and workers to ensure the smooth running of these activities. With limited resources, such as funding and staffing, schools may struggle to provide a diverse range of activities that cater to the interests and abilities of all students. For example, a small school with limited resources may only be able to offer a handful of after-school activities, limiting the choices available to students and further exacerbating the issue of disinterest and disengagement.
Instead of making after-school participation mandatory, schools should focus on providing a wide range of optional activities that cater to different interests and abilities. By offering a variety of options, students are more likely to find an activity they are passionate about and motivated to participate in, resulting in increased engagement and personal growth. Additionally, schools should invest in expanding funding and resources for extracurricular activities to ensure a diverse and inclusive range of options for students.
In conclusion, making after-school participation mandatory for every student is not a viable solution as it poses challenges in terms of time management, individual interests, and resource limitations. It is crucial for schools to recognize the importance of extracurricular activities in promoting personal growth but to also ensure that students have the freedom to choose activities that align with their passions and interests. By offering a diverse range of optional activities and allocating adequate resources, schools can create an environment that fosters student engagement and overall well-being.

They are thought to have originated from ancient bacteria that were engulfed by early eukaryotic cells but were not digested. As a result, they formed a symbiotic relationship with the host cell. Mitochondria have their own DNA, which is separate from the cell's nuclear DNA. The DNA present in mitochondria is circular, like that of bacteria, and contains genes that code for proteins involved in oxidative phosphorylation. 
The reason why mitochondria need their own DNA is primarily due to their evolutionary history. Mitochondria are believed to have evolved from free-living bacteria and gradually lost most of their genes as they integrated into the host cell. Nevertheless, they retained a small subset of genes involved in their own replication and energy production. Thus, mitochondrial DNA plays a crucial role in the proper functioning of mitochondria. 
Another reason why mitochondria need their own DNA is that they possess a unique genetic system that differs from the cell's nuclear DNA. The mitochondrial genome is maternally inherited and is present in multiple copies within each cell. Mutations in mitochondrial DNA can cause a variety of diseases due to a decrease in energy production or impaired mitochondrial function. These types of diseases can be inherited or may be spontaneous mutations that occur during cell division.
In summary, the mitochondria's origin as an endosymbiont explains the need for them to have retained their own DNA, which is critical for their proper functioning. Mitochondrial DNA also possesses a unique genetic system and plays a vital role in energy production. Mutations in mitochondrial DNA can lead to a variety of diseases that are especially problematic due to the vital importance of mitochondria in the cell's energy metabolism.

In real life, there isn't a single physical "core" or "nexus" hub that routes every packet of traffic on the internet. Instead, the internet is a vast, interconnected network of networks, composed of millions of private and public networks, interconnected through a variety of routing technologies. At the heart of this network are Internet Exchange Points (IXPs), which serve as key connection points for different networks to exchange traffic. However, it's important to note that there isn't a single, centralized entity that controls the entire internet.

IXPs are essentially large-scale network interconnection facilities, where multiple Internet Service Providers (ISPs) and Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) connect and exchange traffic. By peering with each other, these networks can reduce transit costs, improve routing efficiency, and increase network resilience. Some of the largest IXPs include the Amsterdam Internet Exchange (AMS-IX), the Deutscher Commercial Internet Exchange (DE-CIX), and the London Internet Exchange (LINX), among others.

While IXPs play a crucial role in enabling efficient internet traffic exchange, they do not constitute a centralized "core" of the internet. Instead, the internet resembles a complex, distributed network topology, where data can traverse multiple paths between source and destination. This design provides inherent redundancy, fault tolerance, and load balancing capabilities, contributing to the internet's robustness and scalability.

In summary, there is no single "Nexus" hub or core of the internet in real life. The internet is a complex, interconnected network of networks, reliant on Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) and a myriad of routing technologies that facilitate efficient data transmission and exchange among participating networks.

Music royalties are a type of payment that compensates a composer or songwriter for the use of their music. They work by honoring the intellectual property rights of the creator and have two main types: mechanical royalties and performance royalties.

Mechanical royalties are paid for the use of the composition in physical copies, such as CDs and vinyl records. On the other hand, performance royalties are for the use of the composition in public performance, such as in concerts, on the radio, television or movies.

The amount of money a composer makes from royalties depends on various factors such as the popularity of the song and the platforms used to broadcast it. Typically, the amount a composer gets for a hit song varies from country to country and according to the type of release format, but it can range from a few cents to several dollars.

As for how often a composer gets paid, it depends on the agreement they have with the record label, publisher, or collecting society. Some licenses have a fixed fee while others may be a percentage of the revenue generated from the use of the music. Payments can be made monthly, quarterly, or annually.

In some cases, a composer may continue to receive payment for their music even after they died if the rights to their work are managed by an estate. However, this varies and is dependent on the specific terms of the contract. Overall, music royalties serve as a way to ensure that artists are adequately compensated for their work and continue to receive payment even after their songs have become hits.

Overall, gas generators work by using the energy from burning fuel to create mechanical energy, which is then converted into electrical energy by an electrical generator.
